It offers apparel for women, men, young adults, kids, toddlers, and babies, as well as jewelry, accessories, and shoes; and beauty products, such as skin and bath care, cosmetics, hair care, oral care, deodorant, and shaving products. The company also provides food and beverage products comprising dry and perishable grocery, including snacks, candy, beverages, deli, bakery, meat, produce, and food service; electronics which includes video games and consoles, toys, sporting goods, entertainment, and luggage; bed and bath, home décor, school/office supplies, storage, small appliances, kitchenware, greeting cards, party supplies, furniture, lighting, home improvement, and seasonal merchandise; and household essentials, such as household cleaning, paper products, over-the-counter healthcare, vitamins and supplements, baby gear, and pet supplies. In addition, it sells merchandise through periodic design and creative partnerships, and shop-in-shop experience; and in-store amenities. The company sells its products through its stores; and digital channels, including Target.com. View More $21M FA At US$113.79, Target is priced as if it will plod along with weak margins and mediocre returns for years. I think that view misses the slow build of higher‑margin income from advertising, marketplace fees, and paid loyalty, plus a real chance of cost recovery. If I am right, fair value is closer to US$174, not US$114.--Executive SummaryCompany: Target Corporation Ticker: $TGT Current price: US$113.79 Estimated intrinsic value: US$174.14 Upside/downside: +53.0% Expected IRR: 12.0% Summary: The share price reflects a business with low growth, thin margins, and weak returns on equity. I expect Target’s higher‑margin “non‑merchandise” income (notably retail media, marketplace, and paid loyalty) plus multi‑year cost actions to lift steady profitability and returns enough to justify a materially higher valuation. What I'm doing: I don't own the shares yet but will buy some soon. --Market Expectations SnapshotImplied long-term revenue growth: 1.4% Implied steady-state margin: 3.3% net income margin Implied return on capital (or equity): 8.2% ROE What must be true for the current price to make sense: Target’s newer profit pools must stay too small to matter, while wage pressure, shrink, promotions, and fulfilment costs keep margins and returns structurally depressed. --At US$113.79, I believe Target is undervalued. The price only makes sense if Target can grow revenue by roughly 1.4%a year in the long run, sustain a steady 3.3% net margin, and earn only about 8.2% return on equity. I think those assumptions are too downbeat. I expect modestly higher growth (about 2.0%) and a stronger profit profile as higher‑margin advertising, marketplace, and loyalty income scales and cost actions stick. On that basis, I estimate fair value at about US$174 per share, around 53% above today.Target is not a “new story” business. It is a mature retailer with roughly 2,000 stores, competing in a brutal market. That matters because the upside case cannot rely on heroic sales growth. It has to come from something more practical: earning a bit more profit per customer visit, and wasting a bit less money getting products to people.That is why the market’s current view is understandable. Recent years have reminded investors that retail profits can be fragile. If discretionary demand is soft, Target has to promote. If shrink is high, it bleeds margin. If home delivery and same‑day fulfilment are inefficient, costs rise faster than sales. Put those together and you can end up with a business that looks fine on the surface but struggles to earn attractive returns through a cycle.Still, I think the market is treating today’s pressures as permanent features. The share price looks like it is anchored to the idea that Target’s economics have structurally weakened and will not recover.The part I think the market is missing: monetising the same footfall twiceThe most important shift at Target is not another store opening. It is that Target can increasingly monetise existing customer demand through “non‑merchandise” income streams that are not tied to selling another packet of washing powder at a 2% margin.Three streams matter.First is Roundel, Target’s retail media business. Advertising is cyclical, but it is also high margin when done at scale because the costs are largely fixed once the platform is built. If suppliers see Target’s customer data and store network as a place where ads convert into sales, ad budgets follow.Second is Target Plus, the marketplace model. A marketplace can add assortment without putting all the inventory on Target’s balance sheet. It can also create fee income that behaves differently from retail gross margin.Third is paid loyalty and related monetisation. Loyalty schemes are not magic, but they can improve retention and lift basket size. More importantly, they make first‑party data more valuable for both merchandising and advertising.None of these has to turn Target into a tech firm. They just have to become large enough, and profitable enough, to lift the blended economics of each customer transaction.My base case: not exciting, just better than “stuck”In my base case, I assume Target grows revenue at around 2.0% in the long run. That is not aggressive. It is simply a view that Target’s newer income streams add a second engine that grows with customer engagement, even if the store base grows slowly.The bigger driver is margin. The market‑implied steady net margin is about 3.3%. I assume a steady margin closer to 4.8%.That 1.5 percentage point gap is the whole argument. It is not a rounding error. On a revenue base above US$100bn, it is billions in annual profit power. And because retailers already run on thin margins, small changes in costs and mix create large changes in equity value.I also assume a steady 12.0% ROE, versus the market’s implied 8.2%. In plain terms, I am assuming that Target can turn shareholder capital into profits at a rate that is meaningfully better than “barely acceptable”, but not implausibly high for a well‑run retailer with scale.If those assumptions hold, the current valuation looks too low. At today’s price, Target trades on multiples that already look compressed: roughly 11.3x earnings, 0.5x sales, and 2.0x book value. A business priced like that does not need perfection. It only needs to be less bad than the market fears.The scenarios: where the valuation can go right or wrongI like to anchor my conviction by looking at the downside first.Pessimistic case (bear): If growth is closer to 0.5%, if steady net margin only reaches about 3.8%, and if ROE settles around 9.5%, then the shares are worth roughly US$119. That is only about 4% above US$113.79. In other words, the downside case is not “collapse”; it is “nothing happens”. That is typical for mature retailers when the market already expects disappointment.Base case: With 2.0% long‑run growth, 4.8% steady net margin, and 12.0% ROE, I get to about US$174 per share.Optimistic case (bull): If execution is unusually strong and Target’s mix shifts faster, with 3.0% growth, 6.0% steady net margin, and 15.0% ROE, value rises materially, towards US$251.What this shape tells me is simple. If Target stays stuck, I do not make much money. If it recovers a reasonable portion of margin and return quality, I do.What I would watch over the next yearThe next set of results and guidance updates matter less for the exact quarterly number and more for what they reveal about direction.I would focus on three practical questions.Is the higher‑margin income growing fast enough to move the group margin? It is easy to talk about retail media and marketplaces. It is harder to prove that they can scale profitably inside a big retailer without creating new costs elsewhere. Are cost actions real, and are they sticking? Retailers can always cut costs for a quarter. The question is whether supply chain work, inventory discipline, and labour productivity show up as sustained improvement, not just a temporary bounce. Is ROE improving for the right reasons? Buybacks can lift ROE mechanically. I care more about whether underlying earnings quality improves alongside capital returns, because that is what justifies a better valuation multiple over time. The risks I take seriouslyThe cleanest way to break my thesis is a world where Target has to keep giving away margin to protect sales.Tariffs and weak demand could keep revenue growth near the market’s implied 1.4% (or worse) by pressuring discretionary categories and forcing more price cuts. Promotions, shrink, and fulfilment costs could prevent any move towards a 4.8% net margin, even if non‑merchandise revenues grow. Competitive pressure from Walmart and Amazon could cap returns by forcing Target to invest more just to stand still. The common theme is that Target’s newer profit pools are not large enough to offset the relentless pressure of retail costs. If that is the reality, then Target probably deserves a low multiple.--What Would Change My ViewDownside: If net margin fails to improve and stays anchored near 3.3% for another full planning cycle, I would lower my steady‑state margin and intrinsic value meaningfully. Downside: If disclosures show Roundel, marketplace, or loyalty monetisation is growing but not profitable (or is driving higher costs elsewhere), I would treat these as distractions, not value drivers. Upside: If Target demonstrates sustained progress towards a mid‑to‑high 4% net margin while keeping capital discipline, I would be willing to raise my steady‑state ROE and accept a higher fair multiple. Target at roughly US$114 looks like a bet that a solid retailer stays permanently mediocre, and I am willing to buy it because I expect a modest but durable recovery in margin and returns that the current price does not reflect.--Resources & downloadsTGT_TargetCorporation_02Mar2026_report.pdf - Download TGT_TargetCorporation_02Mar2026_model.xlsx - Download Trailing total returns as of 4/1/2026, which may include dividends or other distributions. Fair Value Dividend Score Hiring Score Insider Sentiment Score View More Reducing 2026 GDP Estimate We have reduced our 2026 gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecast to 2.3% from 2.5%. Our outlook for consumer spending is slightly lower based on the surge in gasoline to $4.00 a gallon, and we expect a slightly larger trade deficit than we modeled previously. These two drags on the economy are partially offset by signs of continuing strong investment in computer equipment and research and development for artificial intelligence (AI). We expect 2.4% growth in 1Q26, down from 3.2%. The three main factors behind the reduction are that consumers appeared more fragile than we expected exiting 4Q25; February nonfarm payrolls were much weaker than we, and the consensus, expected; and elevated gasoline prices will be a drag on spending. The impact of high gas prices is somewhat muted in 1Q because the attacks on Iran started at the end of February, and the higher prices will take time to start affecting consumers. Households are seeing bigger tax returns, but any benefits to 1Q and 2Q spending may be used to offset fuel prices before they are spent. We expect 2.4% GDP growth in 2Q26, followed by 2.3% and 2.2% quarterly growth for the remaining two quarters of 2026. We are raising our 2027 estimate to 2.0% from 1.8%. We are reducing our dollar estimate for 2027, but it has an easier comparison against our reduction to 2026 GDP. We expect Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation to surpass 3% in March 2026. With the Fed temporarily on the sidelines assessing risks to both sides of its dual mandate, bond traders have taken the 10-year Treasury yield up 40 basis points to 4.36%. That has pulled mortgage rates back above 6%. While our growth estimates are positive amid solid corporate earnings, unemployment at just 4.4, and the assumption that war in Iran will end in the not-too-distant future, the economic risks will build each week that gasoline prices are near or above $4 per gallon. Can GDP's Engine Run on $4 Gas? The Bureau of Economic Analysis will provide its second estimate of 4Q GDP this morning. When we review the release, our focus will be on looking ahead, not back, as we assess the resilience of consumer spending and business investment amid oil-supply disruptions that could raise inflation and reduce output. We acknowledge that trying to gauge small changes in prices and output is trivial when a war is impacting millions of lives. According to the advance estimate released in February, 4Q GDP grew at an annualized rate of 1.4%. That was a deceleration from 4.4% growth in the third quarter. Last year's government shutdown played a role, but that is in the past. Looking forward, the data on business investment looks strong and should drive productivity gains. Investment grew 3.8% in 4Q based on the advance estimate. Spending on artificial intelligence continued to be an important driver of growth. Intellectual property products grew 7.4%, helped by software and R&D. Equipment grew 3.2% on top of 5.2%, 8.5%, and 21.4% growth in the prior three quarters, boosted by information-processing equipment. Based on the Atlanta Fed's Nowcast, the near-term prospects for AI investment look strong. Equipment is projected to grow 8.1% in 1Q and intellectual property is projected to be up 5.9%. The data on consumers is less emphatic. Fourth-quarter spending rose 2.4% based on the advance report. That was a slowdown from 3.5% in 3Q. The huge services category was up a solid 3.4% in 4Q and looks fine. The ISM services index showed expansion in January and February. Within goods, durables were down 0.9% in 4Q. There was a drag from motor vehicles and parts. We do not see a surge in 1Q vehicle sales with two months already reported. Non-durables were up 0.4% in 4Q as real disposable personal income rose just 0.1%. The 1Q Nowcast for personal consumption slowed to an acceptable 1.8% from 3.0% after reports on January retail sales and February employment. Consumers have been a resilient engine for the economy through a year of tariffs. Tax returns will help. We hope consumers don't need to face on $4 or $5 gas for long. Raising target price to $145 from $125 Target Corp. is the second-biggest U.S. discount retailer. It differentiates itself by selling stylish products at reasonable prices. The company has partnerships with an evolving group of designers. Based in Minneapolis, Target ended FY26 with 1,995 stores in the U.S., with a total of 251 million square feet. Target sold its in-store pharmacies to CVS Health Corp. in December 2015. For the fiscal year ended January 31, 2026, the company had total revenues of $104.8 billion, including more than $30 billion from Target's own brands. Sales originated on Target.com represented about 20.6% of the total in FY26, up from 19.6% a year earlier and 8.8% in prepandemic FY20. The company's fiscal year ends on the Saturday closest to January 31. Approximately 28% of merchandise sales came from beauty and household essentials, 15% from hardlines, 15% from apparel and accessories, 15% from home products, and 24% from food. Target was moved to the Consumer Staples sector from Consumer Discretionary in 2023. Developments in the Middle East remain the major catalyst for share prices, Developments in the Middle East remain the major catalyst for share prices, and the uncertainty and growing scope of the conflict pushed stocks lower and oil prices higher yet again on Thursday. Meanwhile, Friday brings new employment data and a sense that a 'bad' report will further depress share prices while a 'good' report may get lost in the geopolitical newsflow.
